title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures
summary: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

title: Bridge: Database-Grounded Interactive Disambiguation for Text-to-SQL
summary: Ambiguity remains a persistent challenge in text-to-SQL, where an underspecified natural-language question may admit multiple plausible SQL interpretations. Recent work attempts to recover the user's intended interpretation through iterative clarification, but typically relies heavily on LLM parametric knowledge for ad hoc reasoning, leading to limited ambiguity-resolution effectiveness and high LLM cost. We further observe that many ambiguity errors stem from ambiguous column grounding, which remains poorly handled. Therefore, we propose Bridge, a database-grounded disambiguation framework built on an existing iterative protocol. Bridge supplies the LLM's ambiguity detection with offline-distilled knowledge about potential ambiguity relations among columns in the target database. Offline, Bridge constructs a Column Ambiguity Graph by first identifying potentially ambiguous column pairs using complementary database-grounded signals, followed by LLM-based verification. Online, columns and values mentioned in a previous incorrect SQL prediction are used as anchors to retrieve alternatives from the Column Ambiguity Graph and an offline-constructed value similarity index, respectively. The results are integrated for further pruning and consolidated for subsequent ambiguity detection. Extensive experiments on BIRD-dev without the benchmark-provided evidence show that, at comparable LLM cost, Bridge outperforms the strongest baseline by 11.60% in execution accuracy and improves the recall and precision of column usage in the final SQL by 5.25% and 12.37%, respectively.

title: Query Processing with eBPF-Offload on Computational Storage
summary: The idea of pushing computation to storage devices has been explored for decades. In recent years, research has focused on computational storage, i.e., devices that allow a host to execute functions as I/O commands on local data. Today, the NVMe and SNIA computational storage standards share an execution model in which the host invokes functions on the device, on data that the host has moved into device memory. Both standards single out eBPF as a format for functions offloaded by the host. In this paper, we study whether this form of computational storage is a good match for query processing. We present the design and implementation of Delilah, a prototype based on an open-hardware device that implements the standard execution model on an actual device and runs eBPF programs calling device-resident functions. As an initial step, we hand-coded a portion of SSB Q3.3 for execution on the device, aiming to integrate computational storage with a database system's storage manager. The series of experiments that we ran showed that offloading gains little over host execution, execution degenerates into column-at-a-time processing, and time is spent staging and moving data in device memory. Because these roadblocks stem from the execution model rather than from the query, we did not pursue integration further. We detail these limitations and lay the groundwork for a different computational storage model better aligned with data-intensive workloads.

title: MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into SQL queries over increasingly complex databases. However, widely used benchmarks evaluate questions independently, overlooking settings where earlier queries over the same database can supply joins or calculations for a new question. We introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) to measure the accuracy and cost of adapting historical SQL. HARE comprises 1,600 requests derived from a fixed pool of 823 verified queries across four datasets. Annotations record which components each request preserves and which edits it requires, distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial reuse. Our method, MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and mappings from domain concepts to schema elements. MEM-SQL uses a layer only if every requirement assigned to it has a match above that layer's threshold. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), MEM-SQL consults the schema only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges retrieved evidence insufficient. Across six language models on HARE, mean execution accuracy rises from 37.1% for Direct Generation without history to 50.0% for MEM-SQL, with 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency on average. Further analysis shows that requests reusing several verified queries remain a bottleneck, with accuracy falling from 56.7% to 29.7%, most sharply when reused components must be placed in a new query structure or combined with a shared join. Applying OSL to three other memory designs consistently reduces generation cost, while its accuracy benefit depends on the memory design. Verified history can thus make generation both more accurate and cheaper, but its value depends on the evidence retained and when the system consults the schema.

title: A Comparative Study of Prompting Strategies for LLM-Guided SQL Query Optimization
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as promising assistants for database tuning, processing execution plans, schemas, and indexes, combined with table and configuration statistics, to propose SQL rewrites and index recommendations. However, existing studies typically adopt a single prompting strategy, leaving its effect on the validity and usefulness of LLMguided optimization unclear. This paper presents a controlled empirical study comparing zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting across GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro using the 22 TPC-H queries on PostgreSQL 17. All prompts receive the same DBMS context, isolating the effect of prompting strategy. Results show that prompting substantially affects semantic validity in a model-dependent manner. Fewshot was the most reliable strategy overall and significantly improved Gemini 3.1 Pro, whereas the 22-query sample could not statistically distinguish strategies for GPT-5.5 or Claude Sonnet 4.6. Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieved the highest validity, while GPT5.5 delivered the highest median speedups among valid trials, with a significant advantage over Sonnet 4.6 under every strategy (p < 0.05); Gemini 3.1 Pro remained highly dependent on fewshot prompting. Speedups among valid trials were relatively clustered, indicating that coverage is the main differentiating factor across configurations. Moreover, some semantically valid suggestions degraded performance, reinforcing the need to assess regression risk alongside correctness. Overall, prompting strategy is a first-class design variable, with few-shot representing the safest practical default.

title: Dynamic Planning for Scalable Data Movement in Accelerated Query Engines
summary: At scale, structured-data processing is often a datamovement problem. Joins and aggregations must choose whether to shuffle, broadcast, or reduce intermediate results, and the right choice can depend on data properties that are hard to predict prior to execution. In this paper, we introduce dynamic planning, a query-optimization method that lets operators choose data-movement strategies at runtime. We have implemented this approach in GPU Polars, where RapidsMPF actors observe table chunks and exchange metadata before selecting a strategy. Controlled microbenchmarks and a PDS-H Q9 case study confirm that dynamic planning makes sensible runtime decisions while preserving both stability and performance.

title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Resource Allocation and Performance Optimization System for Multi-Tenant SaaS Applications.
summary: Multi-tenant Software-as-a-Service platforms face a persistent tension between resource efficiency and tenant isolation, because shared infrastructure must simultaneously satisfy heterogeneous performance expectations, security boundaries, and cost constraints. This research designs and develops an AI-based resource allocation and performance optimization system that addresses this tension through predictive, adaptive, and tenant-aware orchestration. The proposed architecture combines a telemetry ingestion layer, a tenant-aware feature store, a deep learning predictor that forecasts workload intensity and instance configuration requirements, and a policy-driven allocation engine that translates predictions into scheduling, scaling, and query-routing decisions. Deep learning models trained on historical usage patterns anticipate demand surges and idle intervals, enabling proactive rather than reactive provisioning, while reinforcement-style feedback loops continuously refine allocation policies against observed latency, throughput, and cost outcomes. The system incorporates adaptive query optimization and distributed inference management, balancing latency against accuracy so that tenants with divergent service-level objectives receive appropriately differentiated treatment without manual intervention. Workload isolation is enforced through orchestrated partitioning that preserves noisy-neighbor containment while retaining statistical multiplexing gains. Security and compliance are treated as firstclass allocation constraints: role-based and tenant-scoped policies gate resource grants, and anomalyaware threat mitigation adjusts allocation behavior when adversarial or anomalous activity is detected, ensuring that performance optimization does not erode the security posture of the shared environment. A composable middleware layer decouples prediction, policy evaluation, and enforcement, allowing the system to integrate with existing SaaS architectures and to evolve as models improve. The evaluation methodology combines simulation of multi-tenant workloads with empirical benchmarking on cloudnative infrastructure, measuring prediction accuracy, resource utilization, tail latency, tenant fairness, energy consumption, and cost per transaction against static and heuristic baselines. Observability dashboards expose per-tenant performance and compliance indicators, supporting operator trust and accountability. The expected contribution is a coherent, extensible framework that unifies predictive resource allocation, performance tuning, security-aware constraint enforcement, and energy-conscious operation for multi-tenant SaaS, offering both a reference architecture and empirically grounded evidence that AI-driven orchestration can deliver superior efficiency and fairness relative to conventional autoscaling and manual provisioning practices.

title: Stylization as Geodesic Navigation on Diffusion Manifolds
summary: Facial stylization asks for a delicate transformation: the image should look unmistakably artistic, yet the person should remain unmistakably the same. Existing training-free and instruction-driven methods often fail to expose such control, either drifting away from identity or producing only weak stylization. We introduce Stylus, a training-free framework that treats facial style transfer as navigation on the curved latent manifold of a pretrained diffusion model. Rather than interpolating in flat Euclidean space, \method refines the interpolated content--style point by lowering a ratio-weighted discrete geodesic energy under the pullback metric, made tractable by a rank-one power-iteration approximation of the Jacobian. This principle drives two complementary controls: content--style latent interpolation for smooth semantic fusion, and self-attention query optimization for spatially adaptive style injection. The resulting dual-control mechanism provides continuous, fine-grained control over stylization strength while preserving identity-critical facial structure, all without additional training. Experiments show that Stylus achieves the strongest identity and content preservation at competitive stylization strength.

title: A Systems Thinking Approach to Quality Management in Web-Based Information Systems
summary: Web-based information systems have evolved into highly complex and interconnected environments composed of frontend interfaces, backend services, APIs, databases, caching mechanisms, and distributed infrastructure components. Traditional software quality management approaches frequently focus on isolated subsystem optimization and therefore fail to adequately address interdependencies and feedback mechanisms affecting overall system behavior. This paper proposes a Systems Thinking approach for improving the quality management of web-based information systems by emphasizing holistic analysis, feedback loop identification, and system-wide optimization strategies. A layered architectural framework is introduced and evaluated through a prototype case study. Experimental analysis demonstrates measurable improvements in response time, reliability, system stability, and maintainability after implementing system-level optimization strategies such as query optimization, caching mechanisms, and monitoring-driven feedback analysis. The results indicate that Systems Thinking provides a valuable framework for identifying hidden system interactions and improving software quality in distributed web environments.

title: Role of DBMS in Business Intelligence
summary: Business Intelligence (BI) converts organizational data into analytical information that supports operational and strategic decisions, yet the reliability, responsiveness, and trustworthiness of those outputs depend directly on how the underlying Database Management System (DBMS) organizes, validates, protects, and serves data. This paper presents a literature-based technical analysis of the role of DBMS architectures in BI ecosystems. It examines how physical storage layouts, normalized versus dimensional schemas, query optimization, operational–analytical workload separation, storage–compute decoupling, database-level security controls, and schema flexibility govern downstream BI outcomes. We evaluate row-oriented relational databases, column-oriented analytical databases, distributed NoSQL stores, and cloud-based data warehouses/lakehouses across their underlying mechanisms and operational trade-offs. We further synthesize a ten-layer DBMS-supported BI architecture in which security, privacy, and data governance operate as cross-cutting layers across data ingestion, validation, integration, warehousing, OLAP processing, and reporting. The analysis demonstrates that no single database paradigm is optimal for every BI workload; rather, effective architecture selection must align storage layout, consistency guarantees, elasticity, and governance controls with specific workload characteristics, latency targets, cost constraints, and regulatory obligations.

title: Trustworthy generative artificial intelligence and large language models for Big Data: databases, mining, and ethics at scale
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into Big Data infrastructures, shifting data-intensive systems from purely extractive analytics towards synthesis-oriented workloads. This survey presents a systems-oriented synthesis of trustworthy generative AI by examining large language models, diffusion models, and probabilistic generators as computational operators that interact with data distributions, retrieval mechanisms, program synthesis, storage engines, query processors, and orchestration layers. The analysis was organized around three complementary dimensions. The first examines the formal objectives and representative computational characteristics of the generative models. The second focuses on architectural mechanisms in distributed data systems, including provenance-aware storage, governance-aware orchestration, federated and confidential execution, and monitored inference. The third addresses system-level trust requirements encompassing fairness, privacy, interpretability, accountability, and provenance. The survey is grounded in peer-reviewed literature identified through structured search queries that explicitly connect generative modeling with Big Data system architectures, using concepts such as lineage, retrieval-augmented generation, and governance as the organizing principles. It synthesizes current evidence on how generative AI influences indexing, query optimization, data mining, retrieval, and knowledge graph reasoning, under computational and regulatory constraints. It further examines evaluation from a multi-objective perspective that jointly considers predictive performance, robustness, explanation fidelity, provenance coverage, privacy budgets, energy consumption, and governance overhead, highlighting the important limitations of existing efficiency-centric benchmarks. Finally, emerging research directions are discussed, including provenance-aware generation, governance-aware deployment, and sustainability-aware scaling, while distinguishing established capabilities from active research challenges in trustworthy generative Big Data systems.

title: DiG-RAG: A Multi-Agent Dynamic Interacting Graph Framework for Document Understanding
summary: Document Question Answering (DocQA) is a crucial task for processing visually rich and multimodal documents. Existing methods using LVLM-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) mainly rely on rigid, single-round pipelines. These approaches face two critical challenges: reasoning failures and visual token redundancy. To address these critical limitations, we present DiG-RAG: A Multi-Agent Dynamic Interacting Graph Framework for Document Understanding. Our system employs a suite of five specialized agents: Planner, Executor, Generator, Evaluator, and Debater. Structured as a directed graph where each agent serves as a distinct node, these agents utilize statebased routing and autonomous feedback loops to conduct iterative self-reflection and refine retrieval strategies. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid extraction strategy that couples chunk-level textual snippets and page-level visual captions. By providing LLMs with these multi-granular contexts, our framework significantly reduces the initial visual-token footprint and enables adaptive compute allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiGRAG achieves a relative improvement of 7.4% in average accuracy over state-of-the-art methods on five common benchmarks. Queries accepted at Round 0 use approximately 4.41K inputplus- output total LLM tokens; queries requiring refinement incur additional token cost. Finally, we acknowledge slight performance trade-offs on purely graphical and continuous pure-text tasks.

title: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling
summary: Batched matching is widely used in drug discovery, software analysis, and social network analysis. Its core operation, subgraph matching, is a NP-complete graph algorithm that has been optimized in the HPC field for decades. As for batching scenario, we find that current subgraph matching systems are unable to leverage the common structure patterns of real-world graphs, thereby missing potential optimization opportunities. In this paper, we propose BMS2, a Batched Matching system with Structure-aware Scheduling. BMS2 incorporates these intrinsic properties into previous general filter-join strategy:(i) in the filter phase, BMS2 utilizes the presence information of special structure for early termination (ii) in the join phase, we exploit the similarity of batched queries to reuse matching results of common structure. Experiments demonstrate that BMS2 can achieve an order of magnitude performance improvement on GPUs compared to the state-of-the-art with the ability to process two orders of magnitude larger dataset.

title: PerfInliner: a cost model guided machine learning inlining framework to optimize performance
summary: Machine learning (ML)-based function inlining has attracted significant attention due to its potential to reduce code size adaptively by predicting optimal inlining decisions in modern software systems. However, the high cost of iterative program execution in these ML methods hinders the practical application in program performance optimization tasks. This work presents PerfInliner, a performance-oriented inlining framework built upon LLVM’s ML-inliner. PerfInliner employs reinforcement learning (RL) to iteratively refine inlining decisions, aiming to maximize performance improvement. To mitigate the substantial overhead of program execution during training, we propose MIR2speed, a module-level cost model that predicts speedup under different inlining configurations. A hybrid search strategy is employed to collect high-quality data to benefit RL training process. Furthermore, we enhance ML-inliner with additional call site context information, addressing the issue of overly aggressive inlining decisions caused by the default call site selection order. Experimental results show that PerfInliner outperforms the state-of-the-art LLVM O3 optimization on AMD Ryzen 7995 processor, achieving an average performance improvement of 1.02% (up to 10.07%) on the SPEC CPU 2006 benchmarks, 1.43% (up to 8.29%) on the SPEC CPU 2017 benchmarks and 1.73% (up to 5.64%) on the CBench benchmarks. Additionally, PerfInliner improves the performance of complex real-world systems, with average improvement of 2.7% on OpenSN and 7.2% on OpenSSL.

title: SAIL: Self-Adaptive Index Learning with Hybrid Models (Extended Version)
summary: Learned index structures have demonstrated a significant improvement in query performance over traditional index structures. The majority of learned indexes use a uniform node structure throughout their index structures. A few studies show that combining multiple types of node structures can lead to indexes that better adapt to local key-set distributions, hence yielding query efficiency gains. Following this line of work, we propose a learned index structure named SAIL that supports a wide range of different candidate node structures for both leaf and inner nodes, selected via cost models based on data driven approximations. We design an efficient construction algorithm that recursively partitions the key-set to be fitted by the candidate node types. Experiments demonstrate that SAIL achieves 2x improvement over existing learned indexes in query time, with similar memory consumption and index build times.

title: The calibration and energy cost of tabular foundation models in clinical prediction
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare decision-making, where predictive models must accurately distinguish patient risk, provide reliable probabilities, and remain computationally feasible for routine clinical deployment. Despite the emergence of tabular foundation models, evaluation has focused predominantly on predictive accuracy, providing limited evidence of their practical advantages in healthcare. This study evaluates the tabular foundation model TabPFN and calibrated gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) ensembles across multiple publicly available clinical prediction datasets. The calibration comparison followed a pre-registration fixing the equivalence margin, an inclusion gate that removed models that had not learned, and an explicit falsifier. Energy was read from processor power counters, each figure tagged by hardware, configuration, and batch regime. TabPFN was better calibrated on all five datasets across four calibration metrics. A saturated dataset carries no discriminating weight, so the confirmatory conclusion rests on the other four. Rejecting the pre-registered equivalence hypothesis indicates a calibration difference favoring TabPFN, rather than equivalence, although the gap was small (mean adaptive expected calibration error= 0.011). TabPFN showed better discrimination on four of five datasets, with a mean AUROC difference of 0.013 and intervals that exclude zero. Decision-curve analysis showed a small positive net benefit at most thresholds. Its modest gains in calibration, discrimination, and net benefit came at substantially higher computational cost. Tree models were more energy-efficient beyond approximately six predictions; per-prediction cost jumped 121-fold with a single configuration flag, and a validated cost model showed inference growing steeply with context size, making CPU-only deployment impractical at clinical scale. Thus, TabPFN’s advantage is narrow and most justified when calibrated probabilities carry clinical weight, volume is low, and an accelerator is available, where cost is characterized by timing rather than measured power.

title: Data-Aware Scheduling of Code Analysis Tasks for Scalable Software Vulnerability Detection
summary: Scalable vulnerability detection increasingly relies on orchestrating large batches of code analysis tasks, yet static scheduling policies treat every analysis job as if it carried identical cost and value. This mismatch wastes computational budget on redundant or low-yield scans while delaying high-risk modules. The present study develops a data-aware scheduling framework that estimates task difficulty, expected yield, and resource footprint before dispatch, and then allocates analysis capacity accordingly. The framework couples three components: a lightweight feature extractor that profiles code units and their historical defect signals, a cost model that predicts analysis latency under varying tool configurations, and a priority engine that ranks pending jobs by expected risk reduction per unit of compute. To keep the pipeline robust when inputs are deliberately perturbed, the design incorporates a purification stage that reconstructs suspicious inputs before they reach downstream analyzers, drawing on conditional generative modeling to stabilize feature distributions. The scheduling layer is also informed by interaction-aware design principles for automated agents that must operate continuously and adaptively in live environments, which motivates the use of feedback-driven priority updates rather than fixed queues. Experiments on a multi-project corpus compare the proposed scheduler against round-robin, first-come-first-served, and severity-only baselines across several compute budgets. Results indicate consistent gains in early detection of high-severity defects, reduced redundant analysis, and more stable throughput under adversarial input conditions, with the largest improvements observed when budgets are tight and project heterogeneity is high. The discussion examines trade-offs between prediction overhead and scheduling benefit, the sensitivity of the approach to feature drift, and conditions under which simpler policies remain competitive. The study concludes that data-aware prioritization, combined with input purification and adaptive feedback, offers a practical route toward scalable and resilient vulnerability detection pipelines, and outlines directions for extending the framework to distributed and continuously evolving codebases.

title: Comparing Policy-Gradient and Value-Based Reinforcement Learning for Epidemic Control under Health-Economic Trade-Offs
summary: Effective Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPI) during epidemics require balancing disease burden, healthcare capacity, and socio-economic costs, a sequential decision problem well suited to Reinforcement Learning (RL). We compare two representative RL methods to epidemic control: the value-based Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) and the policy-gradient Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). RL agents observe routine surveillance signals and choose among discrete interventions levels, receiving rewards that penalize both health outcomes and economic disruption. We evaluate the learned policies against pseudo-optimal open-loop baselines across several epidemiologically meaningful scenarios, varying the relative weight assigned to indirect economic costs. PPO consistently outperforms or matches DDQN and pseudo-optimal open-loop baselines, achieving lower combined health-economic loss and producing smoother, more interpretable intervention trajectories.

title: Leveraging Memory for Efficient Gossip-Based Decentralized Federated Learning
summary: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) relies exclusively on local communication among neighboring clients to coordinate model updates, making efficient consensus a key challenge. However, faster consensus alone is insufficient under heterogeneous data and realistic communication topologies, where consensus and optimization are tightly coupled. We propose a multistep gossip mechanism that performs several gossip exchanges between two local training updates. By combining multiple model versions through age-dependent weighting, the proposed method exploits historical information to accelerate consensus without increasing the communication budget. Experiments on a non-IID benchmark with a bridge-constrained topology show faster convergence and higher final accuracy than existing methods. In particular, the proposed approach reaches the same accuracy targets 11-14× faster than the best existing mixing rule when computation dominates the round time, and 5-6× faster when communication and computation costs are comparable.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Secure Healthcare Data: A Sensitivity-Aware Selective Encryption Framework for Cross-Institutional Clinical Model …
summary: Federated learning (FL) lets hospitals train a shared model without pooling patient records, but exchanged updates can still leak sensitive information, and homomorphic encryption (HE) of every parameter is costly for resource-limited clinical sites. This paper proposes SASHE-FL, a sensitivity-aware selective HE framework for cross-silo healthcare FL. Sites use SCAFFOLD-style local training and encrypt, with the CKKS scheme, a jointly agreed top-p fraction of parameters ranked by a label-sensitivity score; the server aggregates ciphertexts without decrypting them. A prototype with real CKKS encryption (TenSEAL) was evaluated on the Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset, split non-IID across five simulated institutions. Accuracy matched plaintext SCAFFOLD at every encrypted fraction (96.5 ± 1.4%). Encrypting 10% of parameters cut per-site upload by 81.5% and cryptographic compute time by 86.3% versus encrypting all parameters. However, a worst-case gradient-inversion probe still recovered inputs (cosine similarity 0.999) with the top 30% encrypted, and failed only when the entire first layer was encrypted. SCAFFOLD gave no accuracy gain over FedAvg. Protection covers only encrypted coordinates, against a non-colluding semi-honest server. The results are a small proof of concept, not clinical evidence or a formal privacy guarantee.

title: Quadrotor Trajectory Tracking Under Multimodal Wind Disturbances via History-Conditioned Hierarchical Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multimodal wind disturbances complicate quadrotor trajectory tracking through partial observability and shifts in disturbance distributions. To address these challenges, this study develops hierarchically structured distributionally robust proximal policy optimization (HSDR-PPO), integrating observation history with separate Kullback–Leibler constraints on wind-class probabilities and within-class disturbance distributions. The resulting adversarial probabilities weight policy updates while rollout collection maintains fixed candidate coverage, enabling history-conditioned robust control without wind measurements or scenario labels. Simulations using a Crazyflie 2X model with prescribed external forces cover five training seeds and eight test groups. HSDR-PPO achieves the lowest mean episode cost and mean physical failure rate, reducing cost by 13.0–19.2% relative to the best baseline in each group. Under intensity-matched colored-disturbance shifts, worst-decile cost decreases by 32.9% relative to Joint-KL PPO. Ablations support contributions from observation history and hierarchical reweighting, while evaluations under unseen chirps, a figure-eight reference, and an extended task duration demonstrate transfer without retraining. A policy trained in simulation configured for the experimental platform is subsequently deployed on a physical quadrotor, achieving a three-dimensional position root mean square error of 0.071 m in a representative 48 s outdoor flight. These results demonstrate improved robustness under the evaluated simulation conditions and successful deployment for outdoor trajectory tracking.

title: Agentic Computing and Services for the Computing Continuum
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly executes across a computing continuum that reaches from on-field sensors and edge devices, through cloud resources, to high-performance computing (HPC) centers. Yet most AI applications are still assembled manually, binding models, data, and placement to one environment and one team of experts. This vision paper argues that the next phase of cyberinfrastructure (CI) for AI should be both agentic and service-oriented: software agents, exposed as composable services, should sense the state of the continuum, decide where and how to train, deploy, and adapt models, act through a shared control plane, and learn from outcomes. We ground the vision in the NSF ICICLE AI Institute, whose plug-and-play CI, model and data commons, control plane, and model-card provenance already supply building blocks. We ask a fundamental question: Can cyberinfrastructure become self-driving in the same way autonomous vehicles transformed transportation? To answer this, we present a three-pillar reference architecture, map existing components onto it, and identify the remaining challenges, including decision verification, evaluation, and cost-aware autonomy, that must be solved to transform today's hand-built pipelines into self-driving cyberinfrastructure.

title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
summary: The expanding scale and complexity of HPC workflows demand elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained concurrency, which serverless computing theoretically suits. However, existing serverless frameworks, optimized for lightweight event-driven applications, are architecturally mismatched for highly concurrent HPC. For HPC workflows, high concurrency necessitates spawning a large number of function instances, which entails substantial instance startup overhead and data transfer requirements. The kernel-based isolation and inter-instance communication mechanisms (via network stacks, cgroups, etc.) cause extra overhead—excessive kernel locks from cgroup/namespace configuration, and prolonged latency from cross-node data copying/serialization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel serverless system architecture tailored specifically for HPC workflows. Leveraging eBPF, we design user-space lock-free isolation and end-to-end zero-copy communication mechanisms, thereby bypassing kernel involvement as much as possible. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that eFaaS stabilizes performance under extreme concurrency, reducing long-tail delays and achieving end-to-end speedups ranging from 1.27× to 3.74× on representative HPC workflows.

title: Accelerating GPU Datalog with Kernel Fusion
summary: Recursive Datalog queries such as transitive closure, connected components, and same generation iterate a rule to a fixpoint while expressing many graph analytics. GPU Datalog engines run each round as a chain of separate relational operators driven by a host loop, paying for repeated sorting, per-round allocation, and a CPU↔ GPU round-trip every round. We present MONOLOG, which runs each round as a single CUDA kernel over one GPU-resident data structure, so a single CUDA atomic operation per derived fact deduplicates, tests novelty and adds the fact together. With the state staying on the device, the whole loop runs on the GPU via a replayed CUDA graph and a conditional graph node. As these queries only grow under edge insertions, a computed result is updated in place when edges arrive. On an NVIDIA A100 this cuts end-to-end time by up to 24× for transitive closure and 136× for connected components over the MNMGDATALOG engine, beats GPULOG by up to 29× in fixpoint compute, and updates connected components up to 40× faster than recomputing.

title: Data Optimization Study of Genetic Algorithm and Machine Learning
summary: The genetic algorithm (GA) is a widely used evolutionary computing method in computer science, management, physics, engineering, and other domains. title: Schema-Conditioned Tree-Mamba For Database-Agnostic Cost Estimation Under Schema Shift
summary: Accurate cost estimation is central to query optimization, but learned estimators must generalize when a trained model is deployed on databases with unseen schemas and data distributions. A train-only SchemaVAE and Bayesian information criterion (BIC)-selected Gaussian mixture model derive table-level schema posteriors from PostgreSQL catalog and workload statistics; these posteriors are propagated through each physical plan tree and used by a relation gate that composes left and right subtree states. On a 20-database benchmark with four unseen-database folds, the proposed fusion mechanism achieves the best aggregate Median, P95, and P99 Q-error among representative baselines, and ablations confirm that conditioned fusion is more effective than hard clustering or posterior concatenation.

title: Adaptive data processing using a machine learning mechanism
summary: The relevance of this topic stems from the rapid growth in the number of heterogeneous and unstable data sources in modern information systems. Under such conditions, traditional approaches to organizing information retrieval no longer ensure sufficient efficiency, as they do not account for changes in the availability of sources, their response times, and the quality of the results obtained. The problem becomes particularly relevant in event-driven architectures, for which there are currently no universal mechanisms for adaptive control of the search process and selection of data sources. title: Probe-Based Routing for Join Optimizer Selection
summary: In optimizers that choose a join-order solver by a size rule, join ordering is an algorithm-selection problem, because dynamic programming (DP), genetic search (GEQO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) each win on different queries. PostgreSQL nevertheless chooses among them by relation count alone, although queries with the same relation count can favor different solvers. This paper introduces two landscape features that a probe computes from random join orders in microseconds per query. The tail spacing describes how the costs of the best sampled orders are spaced, and the crossover surprise describes how far the cost of a crossover child deviates from the mean cost of its parents. The router clusters training queries by these features and the relation count, assigns a solver to every cluster that this solver wins in total end-to-end time by a margin, and leaves all other queries to PostgreSQL's default rule. On JOB and IMDb-CEB, the router lowers mean end-to-end time relative to the default rule, and on IMDb-CEB the probe features nearly double the gain obtained from the relation count alone, so they carry information about the queries that the relation count lacks.

title: Machine learning in fiber-reinforced composites: A review of modeling, lifecycle applications, and challenges
summary: Fiber-reinforced composites (FRCs) are critical in aerospace, automotive, and deep-sea infrastructure. However, their multi-scale heterogeneity poses significant challenges to traditional methods. Machine learning (ML) offers a transformative approach for FRC lifecycle management. This review systematically examines recent ML advancements in the FRC domain, covering data acquisition, model architectures, lifecycle applications, and challenges toward industrial deployment. Statistical analysis reveals textual data constitutes approximately 3.2 times the volume of image data, primarily from experimental testing, numerical simulation, and stochastic modeling, underscoring the necessity of multi-source data fusion. Three advanced models are critically reviewed: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), optimization algorithm-fused neural networks (OAFNNs), and ensemble learning models (ELMs). Their applications are analyzed across lifecycle dimensions: structural design and performance prediction, manufacturing and machining process optimization, and damage detection with structural health monitoring. Key challenges include data scarcity, generalization under distribution shifts, the simulation-to-reality gap, and limited cross-material and cross-environment validation, alongside issues of computational cost, model interpretability, and uncertainty quantification. Finally, future directions are outlined, encompassing next-generation physics-data hybrid methods, multi-source heterogeneous integration, integrated digital twin and self-sensing systems, and enabling technologies for industrial deployment. This review provides a comprehensive technical reference for transitioning ML from laboratory validation toward reliable engineering deployment.

title: A Cost-Effective Zero-Knowledge Proof-Enabled Framework for Verifiable Collaborative Learning in Resource-Constrained Digital Twin Networks
summary: Digital twin networks (DTNs) continue to rely on collaborative learning to facilitate improved performance across distributed users. Ensuring model updates integrity and trust in such settings, however, remains a critical challenge, particularly in the presence of malicious participants. While zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) offer strong guarantees for verifiable computation, the associated high computational and energy overhead make such approaches impractical for resource-constrained clients. This paper thus proposes a cost-effective zero-knowledge verification framework for DTNs. The design adopts a lightweight client-side commitment with server-side ZKP-enabled security to support learning within DTNs. To further reduce overhead, a probabilistic proving mechanism is introduced with an adaptive control strategy to dynamically optimize verification frequency. A comprehensive cost model, as well as overall system efficiency, is then developed for the system. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly reduces cost compared to conventional ZKP approaches while meeting the required threat detection accuracy and high system efficiency. The framework offers a practical pathway toward secure and scalable federated intelligence in next-generation DTNs.

title: How Reliable Is Learned Cardinality Estimation? A Data Model-Centric Analysis and Empirical Study
summary: Learning-based cardinality estimation (CE) has emerged as a promising alternative to statistics-based techniques. Yet its reliability remains an open question: directional bias, upper-tail risk, and degradation under data or workload shifts. Existing works typically organize learned CE by learning paradigm, such as query-driven versus data-driven, which can obscure how the underlying data model constrains estimator design and reliability. We adopt a data model-centric perspective, introducing a unified analytical framework spanning query encoding, data feature extraction, and model adaptation. We argue that the most informative classification axis shifts across data models: primary modeling target for relational CE, topology-handling strategy for graph CE, and cross-model integration strategy for multi-model CE. A relational case study grounds this analysis: a topmost-join probe of PostgreSQL reveals systematic underestimation; a five-seed evaluation with checkpoint reuse across workloads characterizes MSCN’s workload-shift degradation; and a matched JOB-light comparison shows that learned estimation can substantially reduce, but does not eliminate, typical and tail errors. We further assess what current benchmarks reveal about reliability and identify open challenges toward robust, transparent, and reliable cardinality estimation.

title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
summary: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.

title: AI-Driven Portfolio Optimization Under Market Volatility and Transaction Constraints
summary: This research examines the problem of optimal portfolio construction in the presence of time-varying volatility, unstable correlations, and transaction costs - all features that lead to performance degradation of traditional mean-variance and risk-based optimization. title: Neural Cipher Bench: Cost and Portability of Corner-ReLU Cipher Implementation
summary: Edge and Internet of Things (IoT) devices run neural networks on GPUs, neural processing units (NPUs), and microcontrollers (MCUs) through machine learning (ML) runtimes. Deep Neural Cryptography (DNC, EUROCRYPT 2026) expressed AES as a bit-exact ReLU network with fixed weights, using a corner-ReLU construction that keeps the cipher inside the affine+ ReLU operators such runtimes execute. What this construction costs on edge and IoT hardware, and whether real ML backends execute it correctly, had not been measured. We implement SM4, ARIA, Camellia, and ChaCha20 (spanning substitution–permutation, Feistel, and add–rotate–XOR structures) alongside AES on a shared corner-ReLU core under one construction policy, derive a cost model for width, depth, and neuron count, and measure five execution paths on four platforms. All ciphers admit bit-exact networks whose width and depth diverge with cipher structure, and the model's width predicted where GPU throughput drops. Every configuration passing the correctness check fell below its classical baseline (best 0.80×, SM4 on the GPU), by hundreds to thousands of times for the S-box ciphers on the MCU, and keeping the activations on chip through fusion raised throughput 1.4–3.5× and moved the peak past the predicted cache limit without closing the gap. Some AES configurations on the Apple Neural Engine returned valid-looking but incorrect outputs with no error or warning, a failure reproduced in a minimal graph without project code. Mathematical bit-exactness therefore does not guarantee backend-level bit-exactness, and exact workloads offloaded to edge NPUs require output validation.

title: SOVEREIGN-MOHAWK: Machine-Checked Hierarchical Byzantine Resilience and Probabilistic Composition for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) at scale requires aggregating model updates across multi-tier topologies while tolerating adversarial participants. A pervasive foundational assumption in hierarchical FL design is compositional safety: if every local aggregation tier enforces an honest-majority guard (eg, Multi-Krum), the overall network inherits global Byzantine fault tolerance. In this paper, we present SOVEREIGN-MOHAWK, an FL architecture and LEAN 4 formal development that refutes and repairs this assumption. First, we present a machine-checked negative result: a concrete counterexample in LEAN 4 showing that naive deterministic composition of per-tier Multi-Krum guards fails, allowing a 60% global Byzantine leaf fraction to pass local filters under concentrated placement. Second, we formalize a probabilistic repair proving that under explicit iid Bernoulli committee sampling, the probability of any tier exceeding its Byzantine filtering threshold is strictly bounded by a Chernoff bound over rationals, verified in LEAN 4 using native_decide for T= 200 committees and c= 50, 000 leaves per committee (Pfail≤ 200× 10− 1000≈ 2× 10− 998). Third, we formalize eight core theoretical developments, including Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) with constructivist rational logarithmic bounds, logarithmic pathdepth routing, MiMC permutation polynomials over BN254 scalar fields, Robbins-Siegmund supermartingale convergence, and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) dual-signature migration non-hijack guarantees. Fourth, we couple these formal artifacts with an industrial Go production runtime and evaluate the system across multi-node Kubernetes-in-Docker (Kind) clusters (up to 500 pods), CI swarm matrices (500–1,500 nodes), and a 1,000-node simulator target under safe (10% Byzantine) and edge (35% Byzantine) adversarial regimes, demonstrating microsecond aggregation overhead (30.63 µs), sub-400ms round latency (373 ms at 1,500 nodes), and minimal accuracy impact (1.8% gap vs. clean baseline). Every formal claim is bound to implementation code via a continuous integration traceability pipeline.
